steps.label: Given
steps.body: The introduction of mass production techniques in modern industrial economies allowed for lower prices because industries could employ fewer workers, many of whom required little training. The lower prices allowed workers to buy goods that they previously would not have been able to afford. But jobs for workers with little training are more vulnerable to elimination than those for more highly trained workers.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The blank comes after "since", so it is the conclusion, and everything before it is the evidence. Let's line up what happens to the workers.

Mass production lowered prices by using fewer workers, many of whom needed little training. Lower prices let workers buy goods they could not afford before. That's a gain.

Then the pivot: "But since" jobs needing little training are more vulnerable to elimination. That's a cost, and it lands on exactly the kind of job mass production relies on.

So one cause, mass production, does two things to the same people. It raises what they can buy, and it makes their jobs less secure. The "But" tells us the conclusion should bring in the downside without erasing the upside.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Predict a modest answer that ties the two together: the same thing that boosted workers' buying power also left their jobs more exposed. Be wary of answers that compare groups the stimulus never compares, bring in new topics such as profits, or turn a vulnerability into job losses that have already happened.

notes.body: The stimulus never compares the purchasing power of highly trained workers with that of less-trained workers. The lower prices helped "workers" in general. Training level shows up only in the claim about job security, so A takes a variable from one premise and attaches it to a different outcome.

Two problems. The stimulus says workers gained something: they could buy goods they could not afford before, so "decreased benefits" ignores the one benefit we're told about. And profits for owners never appear; the stimulus says owners could lower prices, not that they earned more. B needs facts the premises don't give.

The only comparison about job security says highly trained workers are less vulnerable than workers with little training. That points toward better security for the trained, not toward "never" having security. The stimulus says nothing about "the highest paid employees" at all, and "never" is far stronger than a comparison can support.

Match it to the prediction piece by piece. "a source of increased purchasing power" is mass production and the lower prices it brought. "also undermines their job security" is the pivot: those same techniques rely on workers with little training, and those jobs are more vulnerable to elimination. D keeps both halves the stimulus set up, and it stays modest. The word "undermines" only says security is weakened, which is what "more vulnerable to elimination" gives us. On a completion that follows a "But", look for the answer that holds the gain and the cost together instead of picking one side.

This is the tempting overreach. "more vulnerable to elimination" describes a risk, not jobs that have actually disappeared. To say the share of workers who can afford these goods is "shrinking", we'd need real job losses, and we'd need them to outweigh the lower prices. Test it: could every worker still have a job and still afford the goods? Yes, so E isn't supported.

why: Accurate but in the em-dash explicit-Standard register; Goal hedged instead of naming the answer, and the notes were padded.

steps.label: Given
steps.body:
- There are immediate short-term gains in crop yield from a single application of certain hydrocarbon-based pesticides to fields on which they have not been previously used.
  - Studies have shown clearly that long-term use gradually depresses crop yield from this initially elevated level.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Start with the structure. "Although" opens a concession: a single application gives short-term gains. The main point will push against that. "We should conclude that" marks the blank as the conclusion, and the sentence just before it, that long-term use gradually depresses yield, is the evidence driving it.

Now read that evidence closely. Yields go up at first, then slide down "from this initially elevated level". It doesn't say yields fall below where they started. It says nothing about costs, the environment, or the pests themselves. So the safe conclusion is about a payoff that shrinks over time, not one that disappears or does harm.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Predict something like this: the benefit of these pesticides fades with continued use. On a completion like this, reject anything stronger than a fading benefit (a net loss, an out-of-control pest problem) and anything that brings in a topic the stimulus never raised (the environment, the instructions on the label).

notes.body: This is the answer closest to the prediction, which is why it tempts. But "uneconomic" means the pesticides cost more than they return. We only know yield slides down from an elevated level; it could stay above the no-pesticide yield forever, and we have no figures on what the pesticides cost. A shrinking benefit is still a benefit, so A goes further than the evidence.

The stimulus is only about crop yield. Environmental damage is a new topic, and nothing in the premises tells us anything about it. Pesticides may well harm the environment in real life, but a completion has to follow from what the stimulus says, not from what we know elsewhere.

Pests never come up; the evidence is about yield. And "unmanageable" is extreme. A gradual decline in yield from a high point fits perfectly well with pests being fully under control, so C adds both a new topic and a much stronger claim than the evidence allows.

The stimulus says nothing about what the manufacturers recommend, so we can't judge whether farmers follow it. Yields could decline even when the pesticides are used exactly as directed. "probably" softens the claim, but softening an unsupported idea doesn't make it supported.

Line it up with the evidence. The "financial returns" are the yield gains: a bigger crop is worth more, so the step from yield to money is a small one. "diminish over time" is the gradual slide from the initially elevated level. E doesn't say the returns vanish or turn into losses; it only says they get smaller, which is exactly what "depresses crop yield from this initially elevated level" allows. When a completion follows a concession, look for the answer that tempers the good news without overturning it.

why: Em-dash explicit-Standard register; Evaluate only labeled the structure and never said what the evidence does and does not show, and the notes were padded.

steps.label: Given
steps.body:
- *Contrast:* mu mesons (MMs) generated by cosmic rays just outside Earth's atmosphere travel at speeds approaching the speed of light, **whereas** MMs generated in the lab are nearly at rest.
  - *Comparison:* a lab MM typically decays in much less time than it takes an MM to travel from just outside the atmosphere to our detector on Earth.
  - *Conditional:* if fast MMs typically decay as fast as lab MMs, then we should detect only about one one-hundredth of the number **we actually do detect.**

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Let's call mu mesons MMs. The fast ones are made just outside the atmosphere and travel to Earth at nearly the speed of light. The lab ones are nearly at rest, and they typically decay in much less time than the trip from the upper atmosphere to our detector takes.

The fourth sentence does the real work. It's a conditional:

fast MMs decay as fast as lab MMs → we detect about 1/100 of the number we actually detect

Read the right side carefully. We can't detect one one-hundredth of the number we actually detect. We detect the number we actually detect. So the right side is false, and when the right side of a conditional is false, the left side has to be false too. That's the contrapositive:

NOT detect 1/100 of the actual number → fast MMs do NOT decay as fast as lab MMs

So the fast MMs don't decay as fast as the lab ones. The blank is about "mu mesons moving at speeds near the speed of light", which are the fast ones. The sentence should finish by saying they decay more slowly than the MMs at rest.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look past the physics words and the prediction is short: MMs moving near the speed of light decay more slowly than MMs at rest in the lab. An answer about travel time, detection equipment, how many MMs there are, or where they come from leaves the conditional untouched.

steps.label: Helpful Tip
steps.body: Don't let the LSAT distract or intimidate you with fancy science terms. You don't need to know what a mu meson is. It's a thing. You don't need to know the exact speed of light. It's fast. We don't even need to know exactly what "decay" means in this context. Whatever it is, we're told it's something that can happen at different speeds. That's all we really need to understand. You could literally replace "decay" with "change color" or "turn into elephants" and still get the correct answer. Try it. The science might not make sense, but the logical connections would stay the same. And we're being tested on our understanding of the logical connections, not the science.

notes.body: The puzzle is that more fast MMs reach the detector than the lab decay rate allows. If the trip took longer than supposed, the MMs would have more time to decay, so we'd expect even fewer to arrive. A points the wrong way, and nothing in the stimulus questions the travel time anyway.

If the equipment struggled to detect MMs, we'd undercount them, which makes the high count we actually get even harder to explain. The conditional connects decay rate to the number detected. How hard detection is says nothing about the decay rate the blank has to address.

This is the most tempting wrong turn, because the stimulus is full of counts. But fewer MMs to begin with would mean fewer detected, and the problem is that we detect far more than the lab decay rate predicts. A smaller supply makes that mismatch worse. The only way out the conditional leaves open is about how fast the MMs decay, and C says nothing about decay.

This is the contrapositive put into words. The conditional said: if fast MMs decay as fast as lab MMs, we'd detect only one one-hundredth of what we actually detect. We obviously detect what we detect, so the "if" part must be false: fast MMs do not decay as fast as lab MMs. "decay more slowly than mu mesons almost at rest" says exactly that, and "almost at rest" describes the lab MMs. When a stimulus hands you a conditional whose result can't be true, deny its trigger and look for the answer that says so.

The first sentence says these MMs are "generated by cosmic rays", and nothing later casts doubt on that. E contradicts a premise instead of completing the argument. Where the MMs come from also has nothing to do with how fast they decay, which is the only thing the conditional lets us conclude about.

why: Sound logic but heavy em-dash register, a confusing statement of the contrapositive and a typo in the Goal; wrong-answer notes were padded.

steps.label: Given
steps.body: Superstring theory is a controversial new theory in physics. Superstring theory is unlike more established physical theories in that it purports to explain the nature and existence of gravity. A major problem with superstring theory is that to test it we would have to build a particle accelerator 100 trillion kilometers long. Another problem is that superstring theory has had no success in adequately explaining why the force of gravity is not stronger or weaker than it is.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Three facts about superstring theory. It purports to explain the nature and existence of gravity, which more established theories don't even try to do. Testing it would take a particle accelerator 100 trillion kilometers long. And it has had no success explaining why gravity is as strong as it is, neither stronger nor weaker.

The second and third facts are both called a "problem". That word carries a judgment, so ask why. Why would failing to explain gravity's strength count against this theory? Because the theory claims to explain gravity. A theory that sets out to explain a force and can't say why the force has the strength it has is falling short of its own job.

Notice what the stimulus does not give us: anything about what the established theories have achieved, whether superstring theory is true, or how hard the theorists have tried.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: There's no conditional chain to link, so we want the answer that rests on what the stimulus says or clearly implies. The best candidate is the standard behind the word "problem": a theory meant to explain a force falls short if it can't explain that force's strength. Be strict with answers about other theories, about truth, or about effort, since the stimulus says little or nothing on those.

notes.body: The stimulus says the theory "has had no success" explaining gravity's strength. That reports the outcome, not the effort. The theorists may have tried hard and failed. A assumes they haven't tried, and it also predicts that trying would help, which nothing in the stimulus supports.

The stimulus compares superstring theory with established theories on one point only: superstring theory purports to explain gravity's nature and existence, and they don't. It never says they explain physical phenomena better. They might explain less, since they don't even attempt that. B builds a general ranking out of a single difference.

This is the trap that sounds careful, because "some" and "at least some success" are weak wording. But the stimulus tells us established theories don't even purport to explain the nature and existence of gravity, and it says nothing about any of them explaining gravity's strength. "at least some success" is still a claim of success, and we have no evidence for it. Weak wording doesn't rescue a claim with no support.

The giant accelerator is a "problem" for testing the theory. A problem for testing is not proof that the theory is false. A theory could be true even if we can never build the machine to check it. "cannot be true" goes far past a stimulus that only says testing is impractical.

Start with the word "problem". The stimulus treats the failure to explain why gravity is "not stronger or weaker than it is" as a problem for a theory that claims to explain the nature and existence of gravity. E states the standard that makes that complaint sensible: a theory that purports to explain the nature of a force is deficient if it cannot account for the force's strength. "deficient" matches "problem" in strength; it doesn't say the theory is false or useless. When a stimulus labels something a problem or a weakness, ask what standard the label assumes. An answer stating that standard is often the best supported.

why: Evaluate and Goal never identified the judgment carried by the word "problem," so there was no real prediction; em-dash register and a joke about physicists replaced reasoning.

steps.label: Given
steps.body: Economists argue that the higher turnover rate of part-time workers shows them to be much more likely to be dissatisfied with their jobs than full-time workers are. Economists also argue that lower-paid, part-time workers threaten to take jobs from full-time employees. But because job efficiency is positively correlated with job satisfaction, companies are unlikely to replace satisfied employees with dissatisfied ones.

steps.label: Evaluate / Goal
steps.body:
Cerrato reports two claims from economists. First, part-time workers are much more likely to be dissatisfied with their jobs than full-time workers. Second, part-time workers threaten to take jobs from full-time employees. Then the pivot, "But": job efficiency goes with job satisfaction, so companies are unlikely to replace satisfied employees with dissatisfied ones.

Put the pieces together. If part-timers are the dissatisfied ones, and companies won't swap satisfied workers for dissatisfied ones, then companies won't swap full-timers for those part-timers. That undercuts the second claim. Cerrato is turning the economists' first claim against their second: the two don't fit together.

Notice that Cerrato never says the first claim is true, only that economists argue it. So the safest completion is tied to it: to the extent part-timers are dissatisfied, they aren't a threat to full-time jobs. Predict an answer saying dissatisfied part-time workers are unlikely to take full-timers' jobs.

notes.body: This is the economists' second claim, the one the "But" sets up to attack. Cerrato's premises point the other way: companies are unlikely to replace satisfied employees with dissatisfied ones, so dissatisfied part-timers are unlikely to take full-timers' jobs. A completes the argument with the opposing position.

Profits never come up, and pay appears only in the phrase "lower-paid". Cerrato's premises connect satisfaction, efficiency, and who replaces whom. Nothing there tells us which companies earn the most. B needs a premise linking high wages to high profits, and the stimulus never gives one.

Follow the chain. The economists say part-timers are the dissatisfied group. Cerrato adds that companies are unlikely to replace satisfied employees with dissatisfied ones. So dissatisfied part-timers are unlikely to replace the more satisfied full-timers. C says exactly that, and its wording is careful: by saying "dissatisfied part-time workers", C doesn't need part-timers to really be dissatisfied. It only says that if they are, the threat claim fails. When a completion answers someone else's argument, look for the answer that uses one of their own claims against the other.

Cerrato never asks what causes the higher turnover. The economists use turnover as evidence of dissatisfaction, and Cerrato starts from the dissatisfaction. Whether it explains all or only part of the turnover has no bearing on whether companies would replace full-timers with part-timers, so D doesn't finish the reasoning the "But" began.

Nothing in the stimulus says when companies choose to hire part-timers. E adds a hiring policy out of nowhere. It also misses the target: the blank should say whether part-timers threaten full-time jobs, and E answers a different question about the conditions for hiring them.

why: The Evaluate/Goal step ended on a wrong prediction (that one economists' claim is true and the other is not) and never named the answer; notes were in the em-dash register.

steps.label: Information
steps.body:
Three statements, and the last one pivots.

1. Comparison: dark honey tends to have a higher antioxidant content than light-colored honey.

2. Rule: the most healthful strains of honey are all unusually high in antioxidants.
most healthful strain → unusually high in antioxidants

3. Pivot ("However"): certain strains from bees harvesting primarily sage nectar are among the most healthful strains, even though they are among the lightest-colored.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The first statement tempts us to link color and health: dark honey has more antioxidants, the healthiest honey has lots of antioxidants, so maybe the healthiest honey is dark. The "However" stops that. Some of the most healthful strains are among the lightest.

Now look for a fact that triggers a rule. Statement 3 tells us certain sage-nectar strains are among the most healthful. Statement 2 says every one of the most healthful strains is unusually high in antioxidants. Put them together:

certain sage-nectar strains → most healthful → unusually high in antioxidants

So those sage-nectar strains are unusually high in antioxidants, even though they are light-colored. That's provable. Notice also what statement 1 doesn't do: "tends to" is only a trend, so a light honey with lots of antioxidants doesn't contradict it.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for the answer that combines statements 2 and 3: some sage-nectar honey is unusually high in antioxidants. Avoid answers that reverse the dark-versus-light trend, or that make claims about most plants or about the single highest honey, which nothing here measures.

notes.body: This is the chain we built. Statement 3 puts certain sage-nectar strains among the most healthful, and statement 2 says all of the most healthful strains are unusually high in antioxidants. So some sage-nectar strains are unusually high in antioxidants. "Some" is all we can claim, since we only know about "certain strains". A leaves out "primarily", but honey from bees harvesting primarily sage nectar is still honey from bees harvesting sage nectar, so A still follows. When a rule says all of a group has a trait and a fact puts something in that group, the trait carries over.

The stimulus mentions one nectar source, sage, and says nothing about what most plants produce. One light-colored example can't tell us about the majority of plants. B needs a count the stimulus never gives.

The only general trend in the stimulus is about antioxidants, and it runs toward dark honey. The light sage strains arrive with "However", as an exception, and a few light strains among the most healthful can't tell us how light honey does as a whole. The stimulus never compares light and dark honey on healthfulness, so C invents a tendency.

This is the light-color trap. If you apply statement 1's trend to these light strains, you'd expect low antioxidants. But the only sage strains we know about are the ones among the most healthful, and those must be unusually high in antioxidants because all of the most healthful strains are. Could some other sage strain be low? Maybe, but the stimulus gives no evidence of one, so D has no support.

We know some light strains are unusually high in antioxidants. That doesn't make one of them the highest. "among the most healthful" isn't the single most healthful, and "unusually high" isn't highest. Since dark honey tends to have more antioxidants, the top honey could easily be dark. E needs a ranking the stimulus never gives.

why: Information step was a garbled code-block diagram, the Goal named only the task, and the D note wrongly called D a contradiction when it is only unsupported.

steps.label: Given
steps.body: (According to some anthropologists) cultures can most effectively respond to the threat of cultural decay by replacing or abandoning many of their traditions so that other traditions may endure. But each of its traditions is essential to a culture's identity.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body: If each of a culture's traditions is essential to a culture's identity, what will happen if a culture replaces or abandons many of their traditions? It seems like this will damage the culture's identity. "Cultural decay" seems like it would be a loss of cultural identity. So, the evidence that we're given seems to indicate that the anthropologists are wrong: replacing or abandoning many traditions so that others may endure is not an effective way to respond to a threat of cultural decay.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Predict that the strategy backfires: by giving up traditions that are each essential to the culture's identity, the culture loses what makes it that culture. An answer can go further than calling the strategy ineffective here, because "each" tradition is essential, so losing many of them means losing the identity itself. Reject any answer that agrees with the anthropologists or carves out cultures where the strategy works.

notes.body: The sociologist's premise covers every culture: "each of its traditions is essential" to its identity. A culture's ability to reflect on its customs doesn't change that. A says the strategy can save some cultures, which sides with the anthropologists the "But" is arguing against.

Chain it. The strategy gives up many traditions. Each tradition is essential to the culture's identity. A culture that loses what is essential to its identity no longer has that identity, so the strategy doesn't preserve the culture; it ends it. That's why B can say "ensure the elimination" instead of something milder: "essential" is a strong word, and B uses its full force. "rather than prevent its decay" points back to the anthropologists' goal and says the strategy produces the opposite. When a premise calls something essential, ask what happens when it's removed. Often the answer is that the thing itself is gone.

Which cultures anthropologists study has nothing to do with whether giving up essential traditions destroys a culture. "all and only" also makes a sweeping claim about who can carry out the strategy, and the sociologist says nothing about that. C completes a different argument.

This is the anthropologists' claim, nearly word for word. "But since" signals that the sociologist is about to reject it, so the blank needs the sociologist's objection, not a restatement of the view under attack.

The premise says "each" tradition is essential, old or new. How recently a tradition was adopted doesn't change that, so losing many recent traditions still costs the culture its identity. E invents an exception the premise rules out.

why: Breakdown was sound but the Goal stopped at "not effective" and never anticipated how far the answer could go; the notes were in the em-dash register and C's note made an odd claim about implementability.

steps.label: Information
steps.body:
In the past, infants who weren't breast-fed were fed cow's milk.
Doctors then advised boiling that milk to sterilize it and prevent gastrointestinal infections potentially fatal to infants.
Once the advice was widely followed, scurvy (caused by vitamin C deficiency) rose alarmingly among infants.
Breast-fed infants did not get scurvy.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Start with the timing. Before the advice, infants who weren't breast-fed drank cow's milk. Once boiling became widespread, scurvy rose sharply. Scurvy comes from a lack of vitamin C. Breast-fed infants, who never got the boiled milk, didn't get scurvy.

So one difference (boiled cow's milk versus mother's milk) lines up with another difference (scurvy versus no scurvy), and we're told what causes scurvy. The simplest way to connect them: infants on boiled cow's milk weren't getting enough vitamin C, and breast-fed infants were. The rise came right after boiling caught on, which suggests the boiling cut the vitamin C, but we don't need the mechanism. We only need the comparison.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: This is a reasonable inference, not a certainty, and that's fine on Most Strongly Supported. Predict an answer saying boiled cow's milk gave infants less vitamin C than mother's milk. Watch for answers that add a frequency, a state of knowledge, or a proportion the passage never mentions.

notes.body: This matches the prediction. Infants on boiled cow's milk got scurvy, a vitamin C deficiency, and breast-fed infants didn't. The comparison that explains that split is A: boiled cow's milk makes less vitamin C available than the same amount of mother's milk. "the same amount" keeps the comparison fair, so it doesn't depend on how much milk anyone drank. The passage doesn't prove A, but A is the explanation the facts point to. When one difference between groups lines up with a difference in outcome, the best-supported answer usually links the two.

B's "potentially fatal" matches the passage, so that part is fine. The problem is "frequently". Doctors can advise against a risk without it being common, and the passage never says how often unboiled milk made infants sick. B adds a rate the passage doesn't give.

Nothing connects mother's milk to gastrointestinal infections. The infection risk is raised only for unboiled cow's milk, and all we learn about breast-fed infants is that they didn't get scurvy. C attaches the risk to the wrong milk.

The passage tells us scurvy is caused by vitamin C deficiency, but not what the doctors knew when they gave the advice. They may have known the cause and simply not realized boiling affected vitamin C. D is a claim about the doctors' knowledge, and the passage gives no evidence either way.

The passage says infants who weren't breast-fed got cow's milk, but never how many there were. "most mothers" requires a proportion, and an alarming rise in scurvy could come from a minority of infants. Nothing supports E's count.

why: Em-dash register; the B note wrongly said "fatal" was unsupported when the stimulus says "potentially fatal"; the Information step overstated which infants got scurvy.
